skill.name: Who is "it"? Following pronouns back
skill.why: It and they point back to someone. Follow them, or you'll get lost.
skill.how: Find the pronoun. Look back for the noun it stands for. Swap it in to check.

steps.say: Writers don't repeat names all the time. They use short words instead.

show.nudge: 'It' is the robot. So who called the robot Snotbot?
That's the short word. Tap who it stands for.

steps.win: Yes! He means Gus. Short words like he, she, it and they are called pronouns.

steps.say: To check, I swap each one in for 'It'. Which one makes sense?

show.nudge: Gus is a 'he', not an 'it'. Try the others.
Swap it in: 'The shed beeped and waved.' Can a shed wave?
That's the pronoun. Tap what it stands for.

steps.win: Yes! 'The robot beeped and waved.' Swap it in, and it makes sense.

steps.say: Careful! 'It' isn't always the last thing named. Swap both in.

show.nudge: Swap it in: 'The bin climbed inside.' Can a bin climb?
That's the pronoun. Tap what it stands for.

steps.win: Yes! The bin came last, but bins can't climb. Always swap it in to check.

steps.say: 'They' and 'them' mean more than one. Use that clue.

show.nudge: Tully is one person. 'Them' means more than one.
Zed is one person, and he did the dropping. What did he drop?
That's the pronoun. Tap what it stands for.

steps.win: Yes! The balls. 'Them' means more than one, and Zed dropped the balls.

steps.say: Here's a tricky one. Swap each one in before you choose.
show: Zed left his ice block next to the heater. By lunch,

options.reason: Swap it in: 'The heater was a puddle.' Can a heater melt?
Swap it in: 'Lunch was a puddle.' What could melt by lunch?
Zed is a 'he', not an 'it'. And he didn't melt!

steps.win: Yes! The ice block melted. The heater was named last, but only ice melts into a puddle.

terms.means: A short word like he, she, it or they. It points back.
The noun the pronoun stands for. Swap it in to check.

card.test: Find the pronoun. Look back for who or what it means. Swap it in. Does it make sense?

creature.name: Tracewhisk
creature.blurb: A spotted-tailed quoll that sniffs every it, he and they back along the trail. It never stops until it finds who the word really means.

encounters.frame: A Tracewhisk is sniffing a note pinned to the bottom ladder of Scaffold Peaks.
encounters.text: Wren found a baby wombat on the walking track. It was shivering in the snow. Wren wrapped it in her red scarf. Then she carried the wombat up the ladder to the hut. Gus lit the fire, and soon the hut was warm. The wombat stopped shivering. After a while, it crawled onto Gus's boot and fell asleep. Gus did not move for two hours. His foot went numb. He didn't mind one bit.
encounters.prompt: 'Wren wrapped it in her red scarf.' What is 'it'?
encounters.success: The baby wombat. Swap it in: 'Wren wrapped the baby wombat in her red scarf.' That works.

options.reason: You can't wrap a walking track in a scarf. Look for what was shivering.
Snow would melt in a scarf. Wren wrapped up the thing that was shivering.

encounters.frame: The Tracewhisk went to the Scaffold Peaks snow concert. So did some guests nobody invited.
encounters.text: The school band played at the snow concert. Mo had the drums, and Indi had the triangle. Halfway through the first song, two magpies flew in through the open window. They landed on the drums and started to warble along. The band kept playing. The magpies kept warbling. At the end, the whole crowd stood up and clapped for the magpies. Mo says the magpies bowed. Indi says they just fell off the drums.

encounters.success: The two magpies. They flew in the window, then landed on the drums.

options.reason: Mo and Indi were already playing. They didn't fly in and land on the drums.

encounters.frame: The Tracewhisk found a ranger's logbook in the hut at the foot of the peaks.
encounters.text: Ranger's log, Thursday. A fox has been raiding the hut bins every night, so I set up a camera on the fence post. Last night the camera caught something surprising. Just after midnight, a wombat waddled up to the bins. It pushed over the first bin with its nose and climbed right inside. Ten minutes later, the fox arrived. It took one look at the wombat, turned around and trotted back into the bush. The wombat stayed in the bin until sunrise, munching banana peels. This morning I found it asleep on a pile of old teabags. I have moved the bins into the shed. The wombat has moved in beside the shed.
encounters.prompt: 'It took one look at the wombat, turned around and trotted back into the bush.' What is 'it'?
encounters.success: The fox. It had just arrived, took one look at the wombat and left.

options.reason: It looked AT the wombat, so 'it' must be something else. Who had just arrived?
A bin can't turn around and trot into the bush. Look for an animal.

encounters.frame: Tully is telling the Tracewhisk about her grand final. Again.
encounters.text: Tully plays goal shooter for the Snowcats netball team. Her coach, Ms Ana, is very strict. Before the grand final, she made the whole team run ten laps of the court. encounters.frame: Indi and Wren stayed the night in the old hut on the top tower. Wren wrote this in the logbook.
encounters.text: Indi and I slept in the old hut on the top tower last night. At midnight, a shutter began to bang in the wind. Then the lantern flickered and went out. I grabbed my torch from under my pillow. It wouldn't turn on, no matter how hard I shook it. Something scratched at the door. Indi crept over and opened it a crack. Two glowing eyes stared up at her from the snow. They belonged to a ringtail possum with a stolen muesli bar in its mouth. It had been living under the hut all winter. We gave it a blanket and went back to sleep.

options.reason: The lantern had already gone out. Wren grabbed her torch next, and that wouldn't turn on.

encounters.frame: The Tracewhisk is reading Gus's lab notes. It is holding its nose.
encounters.text: Gus's lab notes, Day 3. On Monday I mixed glue, borax and a spoonful of Mo's leftover custard to make a brand-new slime. I poured the mixture into a jam jar and screwed the lid on tight. Then I put the jar on the shelf above the heater, because slime grows faster in the warmth. On Tuesday the slime had doubled in size. It had pushed the lid off and was oozing down the side of the jar like lava. By this morning, it had dripped all the way down onto the heater. The heater was still switched on, so the bottom of the slime had baked into a hard, crunchy crust. The whole hut smelled like burnt pudding. Mo walked in, sniffed the air and asked what was for dessert. I have now put a warning sign on the shelf. It says: DO NOT TOUCH. DO NOT SNIFF. DO NOT EAT, MO.
encounters.prompt: 'By this morning, it had dripped all the way down onto the heater.' What is 'it'?
encounters.success: The slime. It was oozing down the jar on Tuesday, and by this morning it reached the heater.

options.reason: Something oozed down the side of the jar. The jar itself stayed on the shelf.
The lid was pushed off on Tuesday. Something kept oozing after that.
The shelf is fixed above the heater. Shelves don't drip.

encounters.frame: Indi painted a mural at base camp. Zed made notes for the Tracewhisk. One is wrong.
encounters.text: Last summer, the rangers asked Indi to paint a mural on the old water tank at base camp. It was rusty and dented, and the paint was peeling off in long grey strips. Indi spent a week sketching ideas. She drew snow gums, wombats, a giant snowflake and even Mo holding a bowl of fish-finger custard. In the end, she chose a giant wedge-tailed eagle, with its wings spread right around the tank. She painted the eagle with a brush on a long pole, standing on the top rung of a ladder. Two rangers held the ladder steady while she worked. They took turns, because their arms kept getting tired. The mural took eleven days and forty-two tins of paint. On the last day, a real eagle flew over the camp and circled the tank twice. Indi swears it was checking her work. The rangers say it was just hungry. Either way, they have asked Indi to paint the toilet block next.

encounters.frame: The Scaffold Peaks observatory sits on the highest tower. The Tracewhisk snuck in for a look.
encounters.text: The observatory on the highest tower has the biggest telescope on the island. It is so heavy that forty climbers and a crane had to carry it up the peak. Last Friday, two young astronomers, Leni and Sol, were using it to hunt for a comet. They had been searching every clear night for three weeks. At two in the morning, Sol spotted a fuzzy green smudge near the moon. He nearly fell off his stool. Leni grabbed her notebook and wrote down the exact time with shaking fingers. The smudge was the comet, sliding slowly across the sky with a long, glowing tail. Leni and Sol named it Comet Snowcap, after the island. Sol had wanted to name it after himself, but Leni won the coin toss. Leni says it will come back in eighty years. By then, she says, someone should really oil the telescope. It already squeaks every time it turns. Leni has put a can of oil on her shopping list.

encounters.frame: Zed is streaming a speedrun from the hut. The Tracewhisk is watching from the beanbag.
encounters.text: Zed's favourite game, Peak Panic, is all about climbing a frozen mountain before the avalanche catches you. Last night he raced two players from the Pine Gully Gamers, a team that had beaten him three times before. Zed had practised for six nights in a row. The Pine Gully players took the lead early. They knew every shortcut on the first cliff, and they never missed a jump. Zed fell behind by almost a minute. In the chat, his viewers started typing sad faces. Then the avalanche started. Snow came pouring down the mountain, and the goats on the second ledge panicked. They stampeded across the path, knocking both Pine Gully climbers off the cliff. Zed, who was still far behind, simply walked around the goats and kept climbing. He finished first by eleven seconds. The chat exploded with goat emojis. The Pine Gully Gamers have asked for a rematch. Zed has asked the goats to join his team.
encounters.prompt: 'They stampeded across the path.' Who are 'they'?
encounters.success: The goats. They panicked when the avalanche started, then stampeded across the path.

options.reason: The stampede knocked the Pine Gully climbers off. They can't be the ones stampeding.
Shortcuts can't stampede. Look for something that panicked and ran.
Jumps are things players do. They can't run across a path.

encounters.frame: A research ship sent this report to the Scaffold Peaks weather station. The Tracewhisk is reading over Wren's shoulder.
encounters.text: Field report from Dr Imogen Hale, Southern Ocean survey. For six days our research vessel, the Albatross, has been anchored beside the ice shelf, waiting for the weather to clear. The crew had played so many card games that the cards had gone soft. On the seventh morning, the fog finally lifted, and the crew spotted a southern right whale drifting near the bow. She was enormous, longer than the vessel's lifeboat, and her back was crusted with pale patches that looked like barnacles. Our team lowered a small underwater camera on a cable, hoping to film her feeding. For almost twenty minutes, she ignored the camera completely. Then, without warning, she rolled onto her side, opened one huge eye and swam straight towards it. She nudged it gently with her head, once, twice, three times, until the cable swung like a pendulum. The footage is wobbly, but it shows something remarkable: a calf, no bigger than a car, sheltering beneath its mother's flipper. We had no idea it was there. Within an hour the pair had vanished into the grey water, and the fog rolled back in. Back on board, nobody spoke for a long time. Then the cook made pancakes, and everyone started talking at once.
encounters.prompt: 'We had no idea it was there.' What does 'it' point back to?
encounters.success: The whale's calf. The footage revealed it hiding under its mother's flipper, which the team hadn't known.

options.reason: The team lowered the camera themselves, so they knew exactly where it was.
The footage is what showed them. The surprise was what it showed.
The ship had been anchored beside the ice shelf for six days. That was no surprise.

encounters.frame: Wren has been watching birds in Snow Gum Gully. She made notes for the Tracewhisk, and one is wrong.
encounters.text: Wren's field notes, Snow Gum Gully. For a week I have been watching a male lyrebird that lives near the creek. Every morning at dawn, it scrapes together a mound of soil and leaf litter, climbs on top and performs. Its song can last for twenty minutes without a single pause. It copies everything it has ever heard: kookaburras, a car alarm, the creak of the hut door and, most impressively, the call of a pied currawong that nests in the snow gum above. The currawong does not appreciate this. Yesterday it swooped down from its branch and landed right beside the mound, clearly expecting to find a rival. The lyrebird simply fanned out its tail, which is shaped like an old-fashioned harp, and carried on singing. It even added the currawong's angry clicking to the end of the song. Confused, the currawong cocked its head, listened to its own call coming back at it, and flew off without a sound. This morning the lyrebird performed the currawong's call again, louder than ever. I am fairly sure it was showing off. Lyrebirds, I have learnt, are not humble birds. Tomorrow I will bring the camera and a thermos, and I will try very hard not to laugh.

encounters.frame: The Tracewhisk went to the Scaffold Peaks Bake-Off. It was hoping for crumbs.
encounters.text: The Scaffold Peaks Bake-Off is held every winter in the hut on the highest tower, which means every contestant has to carry a cake up four ladders. This year there were six bakers and three judges. The judges arrived early, wrapped in so many scarves that only their eyes were visible. They sat at a long table by the stove, sharpening pencils and looking stern. The bakers came up one at a time, gripping their cake tins with one hand and the ladder with the other. By the time they reached the top, most of them were red-faced and puffing. Mo's entry, a fish-finger sponge with custard icing, arrived lopsided and slightly frozen. The judges tasted it in total silence. Then they each wrote a single word on a card: BRAVE, BRAVER and NO. In the end, the trophy went to a quiet baker called Hamish, whose lemon tart had survived the climb without a crack. Hamish said the secret was a very tight lid and a very slow climb. The other bakers clapped warmly, though several of them were still trying to get feeling back into their fingers. Next year, the judges have asked for a lift.

At the time, few supporters had heard of him, and even the captain had never seen him play.
In his first match, however, he kicked seven goals against the Ridgeback Rams.
Their coach was so rattled that he swapped his defenders three times in the final quarter.
None of them could stop the newcomer, and by full-time the Snowcats had won by forty points.

encounters.frame: Every climber on Scaffold Peaks knows this legend. The Tracewhisk refuses to go near the ninth rung.
encounters.text: Every climber at Scaffold Peaks has heard the story of the Ninth Rung. Halfway up the oldest ladder on the island, the story goes, one rung is colder than all the others, and anyone who stops there will hear music. Some say the music is a ghost; others say it is only the wind. Last winter, Indi decided to test the legend for herself. She climbed the ladder at dusk with Zed, a thermos of soup and a notebook full of questions. Sure enough, the ninth rung was icy to the touch, even through her gloves. When she paused there, a faint, tinkling tune drifted up from somewhere beneath them. Zed, who was two rungs below, swore he could hear nothing but the wind. Indi climbed back down, following the sound, until she found a narrow crack in the rock beside the ladder. Wedged deep inside was a tiny music box, its lid rusted half open. Somebody must have dropped it decades ago. Every time the wind blew across the crack, the little cylinder inside turned and played a few notes. Indi left the box exactly where it was. She told nobody except Zed, and Zed promised to keep quiet. Some legends, she decided, deserve to keep going.
